subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Save More Tomorrow
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Save More Tomorrow.

hook.text: Ask someone to save 10% now and they refuse. Ask them to save 10% starting next year and they agree.

buildup.text: Thaler and Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow program commits employees to raise savings rates with each future raise.

discovery.text: It works because you never see your take-home pay decrease. The raise absorbs the increase. Loss aversion is bypassed.

twist.text: In the first trial, savings rates went from 3.5% to 13.6% over four years.

climax.text: Save More Tomorrow proves that timing and framing matter more than motivation. Make it future, automatic, and painless.

punchline.text: Commit your future raise now. You won't miss it.

quiz.question: Why does Save More Tomorrow work?
options: Contributions increase with future raises, so take-home pay never drops
It forces people to save against their will

details.summary: Save More Tomorrow is a retirement program designed by Thaler and Benartzi where employees commit in advance to saving a portion of future raises. It overcomes present bias by making the sacrifice future rather than immediate, and loss aversion by tying increases to gains.
details.whyItMatters: Save More Tomorrow dramatically increased retirement savings by working with human psychology rather than against it. It demonstrates that smart design can solve behavioral problems without restricting choice or requiring willpower.
takeaways: Pre-committing to save future raises avoids present-moment sacrifice
Savings increase with raises so take-home pay never decreases
Participants tripled their savings rate over four years without feeling deprived

faq.question: How does Save More Tomorrow overcome present bias?
faq.answer: The commitment happens today but the sacrifice is deferred to the future. People are far more willing to agree to future saving than immediate saving because present bias makes distant costs feel trivial. By the time the saving begins, inertia keeps it going.

faq.question: How effective was the Save More Tomorrow program?
faq.answer: In the original implementation, participants went from a 3.5 percent saving rate to 13.6 percent over four annual raises. Most importantly, the vast majority stayed in the program, demonstrating that once the commitment was made, inertia worked in their favor.
